newsitem.title: USA: Trans-World says U.S. government talks helpful.
newsitem.headline: Trans-World says U.S. government talks helpful.

text.p: Trans-World Group said talks with U.S. government officials on Monday were positive and helpful to the company's cause to clear its name and safeguard aluminum assets in Russia.
"The meeting was extraordinarily positive. The meeting went very well," Tyrone Fahner, Trans-World's attorney, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Trans-World talked to seven officials from the U.S. Commerce and State Departments involved with Russia's economy and metals sector, and who are in contact with the Gore-Chernomyrdin Commission whose aim is to foster international trade and investment in Russia.
"They (Commerce and State) know that what we are doing is right for the purposes of the Commission and we expect them to let their (Russian) counterparts on the Commission know that," Fahner said.
State Department officials told Trans-World they were concerned about any threat to investment in Russia because already investment in China was ten times more than in Russia.
Trans-World has many arrangements with U.S. companies regarding marketing joint ventures and raising capital.
The company also had direct contacts with a senior assistant to U.S. Vice President Al Gore. Gore and Russian premier Viktor Chernomyrdin head the eponymous Commission.
"We have also had telephone calls from Commission members interested in our story and offering their support," Fahner said.
On Tuesday Russian Interior Minister, Anatoly Kulikov said there was no question of confiscating any foreign property in the aluminum industry but a probe into the sector will continue.

Last Friday Interfax news agency quoted Russia's Prosecutor General's press office saying it was activating a probe, originally begun by the Interior Ministry, into what it called crimes in the aluminum sector.
Russian president Boris Yeltsin's economic issues advisor, Mikhail Delyagin said Tuesday said the probe into the aluminum sector would continue to eliminate corruption and foster fair competition.
Delyagin repeated Kulikov's view that no private property would be confiscated.

Trans-World's chairman, David Reuben said in a telephone interview Tuesday,"I have never been the target of any probe, anywhere in the world. I have not been in the past, I hope I am not in the present, and I assure you I will not be in the future."
Trans-World dismissed any involvement in wrongdoing in the Russian aluminum sector.
Fahner reiterated that the Federal Bureau of Investigation has told the State Department that Trans-World was not the subject of any probe.
Trans-World is worried Russia might slap duties on imports of raw materials for aluminum production. This could prompt other countries such as the U.S. to follow suit, the company said last week.
Trans-World imports alumina into Russia to toll into metal.
The company is also fighting in Moscow's federal court to have a 29 percent stake in the Krasnoyarsk smelter re-listed.

But despite past allegations and current blaze of publicity, Reuben said Trans-World was no having difficulty raising the $500 million needed to upgrade and expand Bratsk and Sayansk over three years. The company's credit rating was not being adversely affected, he added.
"Some $80 or $90 million is available to us right away," Reuben said. Work has already began on the Bratsk potlines. "We don't feel any problems in raising the money because there is a return on it."
((Huw Jones, New York Commodity Desk, 212-859-1646))
